meta.title: Who really said "Einstein, stop telling God what to do"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Bohr never wrote “Einstein, stop telling God what to do.” His own 1949 account gives a more cautious reply to Einstein’s dice remark. The quip is a paraphrase.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Einstein, stop telling God what to do'?
meta.ogDescription: The famous Bohr comeback to Einstein’s “God does not play dice” is a later paraphrase. Bohr’s own 1949 account of his reply is far more measured.

answer.label: Not Niels Bohr’s words — a popular paraphrase
answer.sourceLine: The idea is Bohr’s, but the wording is not. In his own 1949 account of the October 1927 Solvay conference, Bohr says that when Einstein mocked the idea of a dice-playing God, he answered “by pointing at the great caution, already called for by ancient thinkers, in ascribing attributes to Providence in every-day language.” No documented source has Bohr saying “Einstein, stop telling God what to do,” and Wikiquote lists the dice version as disputed.

source.heading: What Bohr actually wrote

docMeta.dd: Discussions with Einstein on Epistemological Problems in Atomic Physics
Not in this text; no documented source found

source.excerpt: On his side, Einstein mockingly asked us whether we could really believe that the providential authorities took recourse to dice-playing (“. . . ob der liebe Gott würfelt”), to which I replied by pointing at the great caution, already called for by ancient thinkers, in ascribing attributes to Providence in every-day language.
trail: Einstein’s side of the exchange is genuine in substance: in a 1926 letter to Max Born he wrote that he was convinced “He [God] is not playing at dice” (Wikipedia, Bohr–Einstein debates ↗).

Bohr’s own account (1949) places the dice exchange at the October 1927 Solvay conference and says he answered by urging caution “in ascribing attributes to Providence in every-day language” (Bohr, Discussions with Einstein ↗).

By April 1985 a punchier version was circulating as hearsay: a UNESCO Courier photo caption says Bohr “is said have retorted ‘Stop telling God what to do.’” (UNESCO Courier, 1985, at Internet Archive ↗). The American Institute of Physics’ online exhibit gives the full “Einstein, stop telling God what to do” form without citing a source (AIP, Einstein and Bohr ↗).

Wikiquote lists “Stop telling God what to do with his dice” under Disputed, with the variant “Einstein, don’t tell God what to do,” and notes that a similar statement is attributed to Enrico Fermi (Wikiquote, Niels Bohr ↗).
source.excerptNote: This is Bohr’s own written account, and it reports his reply only in indirect speech. It contains no sentence like “Einstein, stop telling God what to do.” The popular line squeezes this measured answer into a one-liner.

sourceLink.text: Bohr, Discussions with Einstein (1949), full text at marxists.org

source.rightsNote: The exact wording “Einstein, stop telling God what to do” has no identifiable source, so no copyright status is asserted for it. Bohr’s genuine account, “Discussions with Einstein on Epistemological Problems in Atomic Physics,” was first published in 1949. That is after 1931, so it should be treated as in copyright in the US.

author.name: Niels Bohr
author.kicker: The real thought behind the quip
author.heading: About Niels Bohr
author.metaLine: 1885–1962 · Danish physicist, founder of the Copenhagen interpretation
author.bio: Niels Bohr was a Danish physicist whose model of the atom and whose principle of complementarity shaped quantum theory. He was the leading defender of the new quantum mechanics in his long, friendly debate with Albert Einstein, which began in earnest at the 1927 Solvay conference in Brussels. He later wrote his own account of those debates, which is the best primary evidence for what he actually said to Einstein about God and dice.

cite.sourceCitation: Niels Bohr, “Discussions with Einstein on Epistemological Problems in Atomic Physics,” in Albert Einstein: Philosopher-Scientist (1949). This is Bohr’s own indirect account of his reply. The wording “Einstein, stop telling God what to do” is a later paraphrase with no documented source.

misattribution.heading: Who gets credit, and why it’s shaky
misattribution.intro: Everyone knows the exchange: Einstein says God does not play dice, and Bohr snaps back. Einstein’s half is well documented. Bohr’s comeback, in its famous form, is not.

items.why: Bohr’s own written account reports his reply only indirectly. He says he pointed to “the great caution, already called for by ancient thinkers, in ascribing attributes to Providence in every-day language” (Bohr, 1949 ↗). The snappy “stop telling God what to do” is a later retelling, not his recorded words.

Wikiquote puts “Stop telling God what to do with his dice” in its Disputed section. It also lists the variants “Einstein, don’t tell God what to do” and C. P. Snow’s 1981 rendering, “You ought not to speak for what Providence can or can not do” (Wikiquote ↗).
Wikiquote notes that “a similar statement is attributed to Enrico Fermi” but gives no source for it (Wikiquote ↗). It is another sign that the comeback floated free of any documented speaker.
Einstein really did put it this way. In a 1926 letter to Max Born he wrote, “I, at any rate, am convinced that He [God] is not playing at dice” (Wikipedia ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The thought is Bohr’s, but the line is folklore. Bohr’s own 1949 account says he answered Einstein’s dice remark at the 1927 Solvay conference by urging caution in “ascribing attributes to Providence in every-day language” (read it ↗). He never wrote the one-liner.

context.heading: Why the exchange mattered
lead: The 1927 Solvay conference in Brussels was where Einstein first seriously challenged the new quantum mechanics, which made physics a matter of probabilities rather than certainties. His objection that God does not play dice was a philosophical complaint as much as a technical one, and Bohr, the theory’s chief defender, answered it in kind.

Bohr’s actual reply was characteristically careful. He warned against carelessly ascribing human attributes to Providence. Retellings sharpened that into a comeback, which is how it now appears on posters, in popular books and on museum pages.
context.detailsSummary: Why the paraphrase is so sticky
detailsBody: The punchy version makes the Bohr–Einstein debate into a duel with a winner. Bohr’s own memoir describes it differently: he says “a most humorous spirit animated the discussions,” and he treats Einstein’s criticism as a valuable prompt for everyone to re-examine their ideas (Bohr, 1949 ↗).
context.pull: “…the great caution, already called for by ancient thinkers, in ascribing attributes to Providence in every-day language.”

In Bohr's 1949 essay, the dice exchange comes in the context of the October 1927 Solvay conference. Bohr writes that Einstein mockingly asked whether the providential authorities took recourse to dice-playing, and that he 'replied by pointing at the great caution, already called for by ancient thinkers, in ascribing attributes to Providence in every-day language'. The essay also says 'a most humorous spirit animated the discussions'.

The AIP exhibit caption reads: 'On one occasion Bohr answered, "Einstein, stop telling God what to do."' It cites no source for the quotation.
